# Day 9: Backpropagation, Training, and Regularization

## Learning goals

By the end of this session you should be able to explain
backpropagation as the chain rule applied layer by layer; implement and
run the standard PyTorch training loop; explain the vanishing-gradient
problem and why activation choice, weight initialization, and batch
normalization address it; apply dropout, L2 regularization, and early
stopping against overfitting; and describe, end-to-end, how Rost &
Sander's PHD method combines every piece of this course's Day 5-9 arc.

## Backpropagation: the chain rule, layer by layer

Day 1 introduced the chain rule; a network with a hidden layer is
exactly a composition of functions, $\hat y = f_2(f_1(x))$, so training
it needs the loss's derivative with respect to *every* weight in *both*
layers. **Backpropagation is not a different algorithm from the chain
rule — it is the chain rule**, applied systematically from the output
layer backward to the input layer, reusing each layer's already-computed
derivative rather than recomputing it from scratch for every weight
individually. PyTorch's `loss.backward()` does exactly this
automatically for a computation graph of any depth — automation that
becomes essential the moment a model has more than one layer, which is
why Day 6's from-scratch gradient descent doesn't scale past a single
linear layer by hand.

**A tiny worked example, verified against `autograd`.** The real
classifier has 192,389 weights — far too many to trace by hand — but
the mechanics are identical at any size, so the notebook shrinks the
same two-layer shape (hidden layer, then output layer) down to 2
inputs, one tanh hidden unit, and one sigmoid output unit: small enough
to compute completely by hand. Starting from the loss and working
backward, each layer's **error signal** ($\partial E/\partial z$) is
computed once and reused for every weight in that layer, rather than
re-deriving each weight's gradient from scratch — that reuse is the
entire reason backpropagation is efficient rather than intractable. The
notebook then builds the identical tiny network as real PyTorch
tensors, calls `loss.backward()`, and compares: every one of the five
hand-derived gradients matches `autograd`'s to eight decimal places.
This isn't just an illustration — it's a real check that the by-hand
chain-rule derivation is actually correct, using the same verification
standard (recompute independently, don't just assert) as every other
worked example in this course.

## The standard PyTorch training loop

Four steps, repeated once per batch (or, for a small dataset, once per
epoch over the whole training set): **forward pass** (compute
predictions), **compute loss**, **`loss.backward()`** (backpropagation —
fills in every weight's gradient), **`optimizer.step()`** (updates every
weight using its own gradient). Running this, unmodified, on Day 8's
subcellular-localization network: training accuracy reaches 1.000 while
validation accuracy plateaus at 0.543 — a textbook case of
**overfitting**. With 490 training examples against a 3000-dimensional
input and roughly 190,000 parameters, the network has far more freedom
than data, and happily memorizes idiosyncrasies of the specific training
sequences rather than learning the general signal. This is exactly the
problem the rest of today's session addresses.

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [Overfitting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overfitting)

## Cross-entropy: why this is the loss

`nn.CrossEntropyLoss()` above was used without explaining why. For a
softmax classifier it's the natural choice, not an arbitrary pick:
softmax's output is a full probability distribution over the 5
localization classes, and cross-entropy measures how far that predicted
distribution is from the true one (all probability on the one correct
class). For a single example it reduces to

$$
\text{CE} = -\log p(\text{true class})
$$

— the negative log of the probability the model assigned to the correct
answer. Confidently wrong is punished far more than hedged: predicting
the true class with probability 0.9 costs $-\log(0.9) \approx 0.105$;
predicting it with probability 0.01 costs $-\log(0.01) \approx 4.6$ —
over 40x worse, for what might be the same single misclassified
example. **Verified in the notebook**: computing $-\log p(\text{true
class})$ by hand for every validation example and averaging matches
PyTorch's own `nn.CrossEntropyLoss()` value exactly (1.203529 both ways).

This is the same quantity Day 4 introduced from the other direction. Day
4's "Statistical significance of an alignment score" section used
**relative entropy** (KL-divergence) to measure how surprising a real
alignment's substitutions are compared to a random background — and
cross-entropy is built from exactly that: $H(P, Q) = H(P) +
D_{\text{KL}}(P \| Q)$, the true distribution's own entropy plus the
extra cost of using the model's imperfect distribution $Q$ instead of
the true one $P$. Minimizing cross-entropy during training *is*,
precisely, minimizing that same KL-divergence between the model's
predictions and the true labels — the same log-odds machinery Day 4
used to score alignments is what drives every softmax classifier's
training here.

- 3Blue1Brown, [But what is cross-entropy? | Compression is Intelligence Part 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GlYgs6v2YfU) — cross-entropy from the information-theory side, building up from first principles

## Vanishing gradients: why activation choice matters for depth

Sigmoid and tanh saturate for large $|x|$ (Day 8) — their derivative
there is near zero. In a deep network, the chain rule *multiplies*
these derivatives together across layers, and a handful of small
numbers multiplied together compounds fast. A concrete check: a
6-hidden-layer network, freshly initialized, one backward pass, sigmoid
vs. ReLU — the mean gradient magnitude reaching the layer closest to the
input, compared to the layer closest to the output:

| Activation | Layer near input | Layer near output | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sigmoid | $8.3\times10^{-9}$ | $2.6\times10^{-2}$ | ~3,100,000× |
| ReLU | $4.2\times10^{-6}$ | $5.5\times10^{-4}$ | ~130× |

With sigmoid, the earliest layer's gradient is roughly **three million
times smaller** than the last layer's — that layer's weights would
barely move under gradient descent, even though it still needs to learn
something useful. ReLU's gradients shrink far less across the same
depth, which is why it (or a variant of it) is the default choice for
hidden layers in modern networks.

Three further tools against this, alongside activation choice: **weight
initialization** schemes that start each layer's weights at a scale
matched to its size, avoiding saturation from the very first forward
pass; **input standardization** (centering/scaling inputs so no single
feature dominates — matters most for raw continuous inputs, less for
this course's already-binary one-hot encoded case study); and **batch
normalization** (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015), which normalizes the
*activations* between layers during training so later layers aren't
constantly adapting to a shifting input distribution from the layers
before them.

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [Vanishing gradient problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanishing_gradient_problem)
- Ioffe & Szegedy (2015), [Batch Normalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03167)

## Regularization: dropout, L2, and early stopping

Three practical tools against the overfitting demonstrated above:

- **Dropout** randomly zeroes a fraction of a layer's activations during
  each training step, preventing the network from relying too heavily
  on any single unit.
- **L2 regularization** (weight decay) penalizes the *square* of the
  weights, discouraging any single weight from growing large; PyTorch
  applies it via the optimizer's `weight_decay` argument rather than a
  separate loss term. **L1 regularization** (Lasso) uses the *absolute
  value* instead, and tends to push some weights to exactly zero rather
  than just shrinking all of them.
- **Early stopping** — simply not training past the epoch where
  validation performance peaks — costs nothing extra to implement and
  is often the single most effective fix.

Applied to the case study: dropout + L2 alone give only a modest
improvement (training accuracy still reaches 1.000 — with ~190,000
parameters and 490 examples, the model has enough capacity to memorize
regardless). **Early stopping** is what actually captures the real
improvement — rolling back to the epoch with the best validation
accuracy (epoch 29 of 100) gives a validation accuracy of 0.590, clearly
better than the unregularized run's 0.543. Reported honestly:
regularization helps here, but it is not a substitute for having enough
data relative to model size — a real limitation of this small,
deliberately simple case study, part of why production tools for this
exact problem (e.g. DeepLoc) use much larger training sets and more
parameter-efficient input representations than a flattened one-hot
encoding.

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [Regularization (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regularization_(mathematics)), [Dropout (neural networks)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(neural_networks)), [Early stopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_stopping)

## The result: training this network for real

The same four metrics from Day 8, now on the trained, early-stopped
model, directly comparable to Day 8's untrained baseline:

| Metric | Day 8 (untrained) | Day 9 (trained) |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | 0.248 | 0.590 |
| Macro F1 | 0.176 | 0.584 |
| MCC | 0.086 | 0.492 |
| Macro AUROC | 0.542 | 0.828 |

Every metric improves substantially — real training, on a real
biological dataset, doing real work.

## The notebook

`notebooks/day09-backprop-training-regularization.ipynb` rebuilds Day
8's exact dataset and model (self-contained, so it runs on its own),
works through the tiny hand-computed-vs-autograd backpropagation
example above, then does what Day 8 stopped short of: runs the standard
training loop unregularized (showing the overfitting above),
demonstrates the vanishing-gradient effect on a 6-layer sigmoid vs.
ReLU network, applies dropout + L2 + early stopping, and reports the
trained model's real metrics against Day 8's baseline. Open it in
[Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book/blob/main/notebooks/day09-backprop-training-regularization.ipynb)
via the badge at the top of the notebook page to edit and run it
yourself.
